title: Compound Interest
tagline: Year 2 — Interest on interest, half-yearly compounding and the CI–SI difference

introduction.overview: In compound interest (CI) the interest earned in each period is added to the principal, so the next period earns interest on the larger amount. The amount after n periods is A = P(1 + r/100)ⁿ and the compound interest is A − P. Compared with simple interest, CI grows faster because interest earns interest.
introduction.placementRelevance: Compound interest is commonly asked in company aptitude rounds, usually with two or three years and with the CI–SI difference shortcut or half-yearly compounding.
introduction.realWorldContext: Savings accounts, fixed deposits, loans with monthly instalments and the growth of an investment are all computed with compound interest.

learningObjectives: Use A = P(1 + r/100)ⁿ for annual compounding
Use the CI − SI shortcuts for 2 and 3 years
Solve population growth and depreciation problems
Find P, r or n from given amounts

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: Simple interest SI = PRT/100. A rise of r% multiplies by (1 + r/100) and a fall of r% multiplies by (1 − r/100).

coreDefinitions: Compound interest: interest calculated on the principal plus the interest already earned.
Amount: A = P(1 + r/100)ⁿ. Compound interest: CI = A − P.
Compounding period: the time after which interest is added to the principal (year, half-year, quarter).
For half-yearly compounding use rate r/2 per period and 2n periods. For quarterly use r/4 and 4n.
Depreciation: decrease in value at a rate per year, A = P(1 − r/100)ⁿ.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Each year the amount is multiplied by the same factor (1 + r/100). So compound interest is a geometric growth, while simple interest is an arithmetic one. The difference between CI and SI for the first two years is the interest earned on the first year's interest: P(r/100)².
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Write the growth factor once and multiply: ₹1,000 at 10% for 2 years is 1000 × 1.1 × 1.1 = 1210. The CI is ₹210, compared with SI ₹200; the extra ₹10 is 10% of the first year's interest ₹100.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Amount and CI
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: A = P(1 + r/100)ⁿ,  CI = A − P
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: n in years for annual compounding.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Half-yearly / quarterly
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Halve the rate and double the periods.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: CI − SI for 2 years
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: The interest on the first year's interest.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Growth and depreciation
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Growth: P(1 + r/100)ⁿ;  Depreciation: P(1 − r/100)ⁿ

mainNarrative: Compute CI by finding the amount first. For ₹10,000 at 10% for 2 years the amount is 10,000 × 1.1 × 1.1 = ₹12,100, so CI = ₹2,100. Using the growth factor avoids computing interest year by year.

For half-yearly compounding, the rate per period is half of the annual rate and the number of periods is doubled. ₹8,000 at 10% for one year compounded half-yearly is 8000 × (1.05)² = ₹8,820, which is more than annual compounding (₹8,800).
The CI − SI shortcut for two years is P(r/100)². If the difference is ₹65 at 10%, then P × 0.01 = 65 and P = ₹6,500. For three years the difference is P(r/100)²(3 + r/100).
If the rates differ by year, multiply the factors: 1.10 for the first year and 1.20 for the second give 1.32. Population growth and depreciation use the same idea with (1 + r/100) or (1 − r/100).
To find the time, compute the factor needed: if money doubles at 10% compound, solve 1.1ⁿ = 2. For quick estimates, the "rule of 72" says it takes about 72 ÷ r years.

deepDiveAspects.title: Rule of 72
deepDiveAspects.content: The number of years for money to double at compound r% is approximately 72 ÷ r. At 8% it is about 9 years. This is an estimate, not exact.

deepDiveAspects.title: CI versus SI over many years
deepDiveAspects.content: In year 1, CI and SI are equal. Afterwards CI grows faster. After 10 years at 10%, CI gives 1.1¹⁰ ≈ 2.59 times the principal while SI gives 2 times.

solvedExamples.title: Compound interest for two years
solvedExamples.question: Find the compound interest on ₹10,000 at 10% per annum for 2 years.

solvedExamples.title: Half-yearly compounding
solvedExamples.question: Find the amount on ₹8,000 at 10% per annum for one year when interest is compounded half-yearly.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The second half-year earns interest on the first half-year's interest.

solvedExamples.title: CI − SI difference
solvedExamples.question: The difference between the compound and simple interest on a sum for 2 years at 10% per annum is ₹65. Find the sum.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The difference is the interest on the first year's interest.

shortcutMethods.title: Growth factor chain

traditionalVsShortcut.traditionalMethod: Compute interest year by year and add to the principal.
traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Multiply by 1.r once per period. Use P(r/100)² for the 2-year CI−SI difference. For half-yearly, halve the rate and double the periods.

rulesForApplication: Compute A first, then CI = A − P.
Compound growth and depreciation use factors.

commonMistakes.mistake: Not halving the rate for half-yearly

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Estimate: CI for 2 years is slightly more than SI; options below SI can be eliminated.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Memorise squares of 1.05, 1.1, 1.2, and cubes of 1.1 to speed up.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: The CI−SI shortcut is a favourite for quick questions.

keyTakeaways: Match the rate to the period.
selfCheckQuestions: Can I compute CI for 2 years without a calculator?
Can I find P from the CI−SI difference?
